'''''Artemisia maritima''''' is a [[Europe]]an species of [[Artemisia (plant)|wormwood]] known as '''sea wormwood''',<ref name=BSBI>{{cite web |title=Sea Wormwood ''Artemisia maritima'' L. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.7mxztr |access-date=9 November 2024 }}</ref> and also formerly often by its [[synonym (biology)|synonym]] ''Seriphidium maritimum''.<ref name = "Streeter">Streeter D, Hart-Davies C, Hardcastle A, Cole F, Harper L. 2009. ''Collins Flower Guide''. Harper Collins {{ISBN|9-78-000718389-0}}</ref> It is native to the Atlantic coasts of northern [[Europe]], from western and northern [[France]], [[Ireland]], the [[United Kingdom]], [[Belgium]], the [[Netherlands]], [[Germany]], [[Denmark]], [[Sweden]], [[Norway]], the [[Baltic States]], and northwestern [[Russia]].<ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=Plants of the World Online | website=Plants of the World Online | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A179785-1 | access-date=2024-11-09}}</ref><ref name="Tela">[http://www.tela-botanica.org/bdtfx-nn-74975-synthese Tela Botanica, Armoise maritime, ''Artemisia maritima'' L.] in French</ref> In [[Great Britain]], it is found as far north as [[Wigton]] on the west coast and [[Cruden Bay]] on the east coast, and in [[Ireland]], on the east and west coasts between [[Dublin]] and [[Killough]], and [[Tralee Bay]] to [[Galway]]; it also occurs on the [[Isle of Man]].<ref name=BSBI/><ref name="NBN Atlas">{{cite web |url= https://species.nbnatlas.org/species/NHMSYS0000463463 |title=Seriphidium maritimum |publisher=National Biodiversity Network Trust |website=NBN Atlas |access-date=February 24, 2024}}</ref>

There are two [[subspecies]]:<ref name="POWO"/>
*''Artemisia maritima'' subsp. ''maritima'' – in the western part of the range
*''Artemisia maritima'' subsp. ''humifusa'' <small>(Fr. ex C.Hartm.) K.Perss.</small> – in the northeastern part of the range

== Description and similar species ==
Sea wormwood is a herbaceous [[perennial plant]] or [[subshrub]] growing to 50 cm, which flowers from August to September; it has strongly aromatic pale grey-green to whitish-green foliage, and is [[Anemophily|wind pollinated]]. The leaves are deeply twice [[pinnatifid]], with narrow, linear segments, and, like the whole plant, are covered on both sides with a dense coat of white cottony hairs. The small, oblong [[Head (botany)|flower heads]], each containing three to six tubular florets 1–2 mm diameter, are of a yellowish or brownish tint; they are produced in August and September, and are arranged in racemes, sometimes drooping, sometimes erect.<ref name = "Streeter"/><ref>{{cite web | url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Artemisia+maritima | title=Artemisia maritima Sea Wormwood PFAF Plant Database }}</ref> 

It is the [[caterpillar]] foodplant of [[Eupithecia extensaria]].<ref>{{cite book |last= Lowen|first= James|author-link= |date= 2021|title= Much Ado About Mothing|url= |location= London|publisher= Bloomsbury|page= 384|isbn=978-1-4729-6697-1}}</ref>

It somewhat resembles wormwood ''[[Artemisia absinthium]]'' and hoary mugwort ''[[Artemisia stelleriana|A. stelleriana]]'', but has slenderer leaf segments under 2 mm broad; ''A. stelleriana'' also lacks the strong scent.<ref name = "Streeter"/>

Reports of the species from southeastern Europe are based on misapplication of the name to the closely related ''[[Artemisia santonicum]]''.<ref name="europlusmed2">{{cite web | last=Soják | first=(L.) | author2=Waldst. &amp | last3=Hegi | first3=Kit.) | last4=Poljakov | first4=Kit.) | title=Artemisia santonicum | website=Euro+Med-Plantbase | url=https://europlusmed.org/cdm_dataportal/taxon/b3a02da8-4936-4a6e-8591-fc1fd383bfd6/synonymy?highlight=16da4c3c-fd75-4457-991f-ddb2e1c1821c#16da4c3c-fd75-4457-991f-ddb2e1c1821c | access-date=2024-11-09}}</ref>

== Habitat ==
It occurs mostly on saline soils, being found on the drier parts of [[salt marsh|saltmarshes]], brackish ditches, sea cliffs, and coastal shingle.<ref name=BSBI/> As with many other saltmarsh plants, it has started to colonise inland along roadsides that are salted to melt winter ice and snow.<ref name=BSBI/>

== Usage ==
[[File:Artemisia maritima baie-authie 80 15072007 1.jpg|thumb|Close up of Artemisia maritima foliage]]
[[John Hill (botanist)|John Hill]] said in 1771 of this species: "This is a very noble bitter: its peculiar province is to give an appetite, as that of the Common Wormwood is to assist [[digestion]]; the flowery tops and the young [[Shoot (botany)|shoots]] possess the virtue: the older [[Leaves]] and the [[plant stem|Stalk]] should be thrown away as useless .... The [[apothecaries]] put three times as much sugar as of the ingredient in their [[Conserves]]; but the virtue is lost in the sweetness, those will not keep so well that have less [[sugar]], but 'tis easy to make them fresh as they are wanted."<ref>{{cite book |title=Virtues of British Herbs. With the History, Description, and Figures of the several Kinds |url=https://archive.org/details/b30500357_0001/page/n5/mode/2up |author=Hill, John |year=1771 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/b30500357_0001/page/12/mode/2up 12]-13 |publisher=London: Printed for R. Baldwin }}</ref> [[Robert John Thornton|Thornton]], in his Family Herbal, tells us that "beat up with thrice its weight of fine sugar, it is made up into a conserve ordered by the London College, and may be taken where the other preparations disgust too much."<ref>{{cite book |title=A Family Herbal: or, Familiar Account of the Medical Properties of British and Foreign Plants |url=https://archive.org/details/b29288642/page/n5/mode/2up |author=Thornton, Robert John |year=1814 |page=[https://archive.org/details/b29288642/page/706/mode/2up 707] |publisher=London: B. and R. Crosby }}</ref>

The plant is a source of the [[sesquiterpenoid]] [[santonin]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Natural Products: The Secondary Metabolites|first=James Ralph|last=Hanson|year=2003|page=85|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K8pgDqX9CIcC&pg=PA85|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|location=Cambridge|isbn=9780854044900|accessdate=2016-10-23}}</ref>
